slide.title: Small, Safe Model Containers
slide.body: A large grey container labelled 'full image' beside a smaller teal container with a padlock labelled 'slim · multi-stage · non-root'. Small tag: MLOps · Lesson 8.

scenes.voiceover: Your API runs on your laptop. Will it run on the server with the same Python, the same libraries and the same model file? A container says yes. But a careless container can be slow, large, and a security risk.

slide.title: Containerising the Model Service
slide.body: MLOps: Deploying and Monitoring Models · Lesson 8 of 18

scenes.voiceover: In the last lesson, our API learned to reject bad input and to log every prediction. Now we package it. You already know basic Docker, so we focus on four choices that matter most for a production model service.

slide.title: Slim base + multi-stage build
slide.body: Stage 1 box 'build': python slim + build wheels (tools, caches). Arrow carrying only 'wheels' → Stage 2 box 'runtime': python slim + app.py + model/. Tools and caches left behind in stage 1 (greyed)

scenes.voiceover: First, a small base image. A slim Python image contains much less than the full one, so it downloads faster and has fewer packages that could contain security problems. Second, a multi-stage build. The first stage installs the dependencies. The final stage copies only the results. Build tools and caches stay behind.

slide.title: Choices 3 and 4
slide.body: 3. Non-root user: limits damage if the service is attacked. 4. Where does the model come from?

scenes.voiceover: Third, a non-root user. By default, processes in a container run as root. If an attacker breaks into the service, a normal user limits what they can do. Fourth, decide where the model comes from.

slide.title: Model inside or loaded at start-up?
slide.body: Copy into image: self-contained · fast start · one tag = one model · new image per version. Load from registry: one image for any version · depends on registry at start-up · needs runtime credentials. Course choice: copy in → rollback = run the previous image

scenes.voiceover: You can copy the model into the image. Then the image is self-contained, starts fast, and each image tag means exactly one model. Or you can load it from the registry at start-up. One image serves any version, but start-up depends on the registry, and the container needs credentials. In this course we copy the model in, because rollback becomes simple: run the previous image.

scenes.on_screen_text: Never put secrets in an image
scenes.voiceover: One firm rule. Never put secrets in a Dockerfile or an image. Anyone who can pull the image can read its layers. Pass secrets when the container runs, and keep that file out of Git.

scenes.stock_query: shipping containers stacked at port crane
scenes.on_screen_text: Pack the product, not the tools
scenes.voiceover: A container is like a shipping container for goods. Everything the product needs travels inside, so it arrives the same at every port. And a multi-stage build packs the product, but leaves the factory tools at home.

screen_steps: Run: python export_model.py and show the output 'exported wine-quality-clf v1'
Show the new model/ folder and model_version.txt
Create .dockerignore with .venv, mlflow.db, mlruns, data, *.jsonl, .git and .env
scenes.voiceover: Let's watch Lars Eriksson, a platform engineer at a hypothetical energy company in Gothenburg, Sweden. First, he exports the champion model from the registry to a local model folder. Then he creates a docker ignore file that keeps out the virtual environment, the database, the data, the logs, the Git folder and any environment file.

screen_steps: Open the Dockerfile in the editor
Highlight Stage 1: FROM python:3.11-slim AS build and the pip wheel line
Highlight Stage 2: COPY --from=build, useradd appuser and chown
Highlight COPY app.py, COPY model/, ENV MODEL_URI=/app/model and USER appuser
scenes.voiceover: Now the Dockerfile, in two stages. The build stage turns the requirements into ready packages. The runtime stage installs them, creates a normal user, copies only the app and the model folder, and switches to that user before starting the server.

screen_steps: Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/health and show model_loaded true
scenes.voiceover: He builds the image with a version tag, and runs it. In the browser, the health page answers from inside the container.

screen_steps: Run: docker images wine-api and show the SIZE column
Show the size of a single-stage build on the full python:3.11 image and place the two side by side
Run: docker run --rm wine-api:v1 whoami and show the output appuser
scenes.voiceover: Next, he lists the image size, and compares it with a single-stage build on the full Python image. The slim, multi-stage image is clearly smaller. Record your own sizes, because they depend on your requirements and platform. Last, he checks the user. The container prints app user, not root.

scenes.on_screen_text: Copy only what the service needs
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to copy the whole project folder into the image. That silently adds the virtual environment, the database, log files, and sometimes a file with passwords. The image grows, and secrets leak to anyone who pulls it. Copy only what the service needs, and keep the ignore file as a second safety net.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Slim + multi-stage + non-root. 2. Model in the image: one tag = one model, easy rollback. 3. No secrets in images; use .dockerignore.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, use a slim base image, a multi-stage build and a non-root user for model services. Second, copying the model into the image makes each tag mean one model and makes rollback simple, while loading from the registry is more flexible but adds a start-up dependency. Third, never put secrets in an image.

slide.title: Exercise: containerise and shrink
slide.body: Single-stage build → record size · apply one technique · rebuild → record size · /health and /predict work · whoami is not root · about 40 minutes

scenes.voiceover: In the exercise below this video, you will write a Dockerfile for your service, build it, and shrink the image with at least one technique. Record the size before and after. It takes about forty minutes, and your capstone will publish exactly this image.
In the next lesson, we measure how fast this container really is, in Batch versus Online Serving and Performance. See you there.
